points.name: Melrose, Mott Haven, Longwood, & Hunts Point

smoke.why: Cigarette smoking is the number-one risk factor for lung cancer and is linked to about 80% of US lung-cancer deaths (CDC). The survey measures current adult smoking, while lung cancer today reflects smoking decades ago, so it is a proxy for each area's smoking history.

pov.why: Lower-income areas have more smoking, more occupational and indoor exposures and worse air. The link is partly mediated by smoking, and for all cancers combined the gradient can reverse because screening-detected cancers are commoner in richer areas.

ins.why: Lack of insurance mainly changes whether a cancer is found (screening, diagnosis), not whether it starts, so the sign is ambiguous: poorer access lowers recorded incidence, while the socioeconomic disadvantage behind it raises risk.

ndvi.why: Vegetation can filter and dilute air pollution, encourages physical activity and lowers heat and stress. Observational cohorts report lower lung-cancer risk with higher NDVI (hazard ratio 0.89 per 0.1 NDVI in a 2025 cohort), but NDVI is an imperfect exposure measure and greenness also tracks lower-density suburban areas.

so2.why: Marker of sulfur-containing fuel combustion (heating oil). Limited evidence for lung cancer on its own, and the NYC series in this project ends in 2016.

o3.why: Ozone is a respiratory irritant but is not an established lung carcinogen. In cities its summer mean is lower near traffic (nitric oxide destroys ozone), so it behaves as an inverse marker of the urban core.

no2.why: Traffic-related pollutant used as a marker of the traffic mixture; several cohort studies link it to lung-cancer incidence, but it is hard to separate from PM₂.₅ and other traffic emissions.

no.why: Fresh combustion emission that converts to NO₂ within minutes. No separate carcinogenic mechanism is established; it is almost a duplicate of NO₂.

pm25.why: IARC classified outdoor air pollution, and particulate matter within it, as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1) in 2013, with sufficient evidence for lung cancer and a rising risk with rising exposure.

bc.why: Black carbon tracks diesel and other combustion soot; IARC classified diesel engine exhaust as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1, lung cancer) in 2012. Few studies use black carbon itself, and in NYC it is almost identical to PM₂.₅.

snap.why: Count of SNAP-authorised stores per km². Mostly reflects how dense and commercial an area is; diet effects on lung cancer are modest and not captured by store counts.

super.why: Better access to supermarkets could improve diet (fruit and vegetable intake is weakly protective for lung cancer). Per-km² counts mainly track urban density.

conv.why: Convenience stores are a main tobacco retail channel, so store density may act as a smoking-access proxy (a hypothesis; the literature still needs checking by the group). As a density measure it also tracks the urban core.

tmean.why: No established mechanism for lung-cancer incidence. Annual mean temperature mostly separates the dense, hotter core from the outer areas (urban heat island).

tmax.why: Summer heat is a health hazard for other outcomes (heat illness, ozone formation) but has no established link to lung-cancer incidence. Skin cancer depends on UV, not temperature.

precip.why: No plausible mechanism. Almost all of its variation is year-to-year weather shared by the whole city, so any neighborhood-level pattern is a location fingerprint.
